Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/handoff

# Handoff

## Overview

A **handoff** is the atomic drovr boundary: run one phase agent, have it compress its own
work into a `<phase>-HANDOFF.md`, then seed the next fresh agent with that doc. This is the
building block `drovr:pipeline` loops over; use it directly for a single boundary.

**The load-bearing move is the finishing agent authoring its own handoff, in-context, as its
final action.** It has the *entire* session and knows what is load-bearing, so it writes the
7-section briefing itself and then signals done — `drovr phase done` refuses until that file
exists. Preserve decisions + interfaces, drop narration.

> This reverses drovr's earlier "fresh reader, never self-summary" design. That design feared
> *context rot* (Chroma: output degrades as the window fills), but the fresh reader could only
> see a lossy pane snapshot via `herdr agent read` — so it summarized the wrong thing (e.g.
> regurgitating the injected seed instead of the phase's real artifact; see
> `forge.ko.ag/drovr/drovr/issues`). A context-aware author of the *complete* session beats a neutral
> reader of an *incomplete* one. Context rot is mitigated where it matters: compression is
> recall + selection (rot-resistant), it can happen at the fullness threshold rather than the
> ceiling, and git pointers make the handoff an index into re-derivable truth, not the sole
> truth. Compaction is one of drovr's three context-engineering levers (with note-taking/git
> and sub-agents — see `drovr:using-drovr`); this skill is the compaction lever.

## Bind checklists to tracked task state

The four steps below are a checklist, and so is the 7-section handoff they end in.

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

## The four steps

Assume a run exists (`drovr new <run> --task "..."` — see `drovr:using-drovr` for setup).
Run name is `<run>`; the phase you are running is `<phase>`.

1. **Start the phase — briefed.** drovr composes the brief (frame, scope, completion
   contract) and injects it; your `--context` is the part it cannot know, which across a
   handoff boundary is the PRIOR phase's handoff:
   ```
   drovr collect <run> <prev> > /tmp/<prev>-handoff.md   # prints <prev>-HANDOFF.md
   drovr phase start <run> <phase> --context-file /tmp/<prev>-handoff.md
   ```
   For the first phase there is no prior handoff — omit `--context` and the run's task
   carries it. Read exactly what the agent will be told with
   `drovr phase brief <run> <phase>`; do not retype or paraphrase it.

2. **Check it landed.** `phase start` prints `briefed phase '<phase>'` on success. If it
   exits 2 the pane is up but UNBRIEFED — re-deliver once the agent is at its composer:
   ```
   drovr phase brief <run> <phase> --context-file /tmp/<prev>-handoff.md \
     | drovr phase send <run> <phase> -
   ```
   `phase send` also stays available for free-form mid-flight nudges; a message is not a
   brief, and you never author the frame.

   The composed brief carries the **completion contract**, whose final two
   actions are, in order:
   1. **Author the handoff.** Write `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/<phase>-HANDOFF.md` — the
      fixed 7-section document (see `HANDOFF-template.md`), compressed from your own context,
      **git pointers mandatory**. This is *your* job as the finishing agent; nothing compresses
      it for you.
   2. **Signal done:** run `drovr phase done <run> <phase>`. It **refuses with an error until
      the handoff above exists, is non-empty, and has no section left at the scaffold's
      `TODO`** — the handoff and the done-marker are one atomic completion step, and a form
      still holding its placeholders carries nothing for the next phase to inherit. The
      error names the unfilled sections.

   Also tell the agent that any reviewers it dispatches must run in the **foreground**
   (never `run_in_background`, never yield waiting on them), so step 3 can detect completion.

3. **Wait for done — background the wait, then end your turn.**
   ```
   drovr phase wait <run> <phase> --timeout-ms 86400000     # Bash run_in_background: true
   ```
   Then **stop and end the turn immediately**: no other command, no edits, no scheduled
   wakeup. The harness wakes you with the exit code when the process exits — that notification
   *is* your synchronization signal. `drovr phase wait` is still the sync primitive; the only
   change is that the harness, not the Bash call, holds the block.

   **Why not foreground?** A foreground Bash call is hard-capped at **600 000 ms (10 min)** —
   you cannot ask for more. Real phases routinely run longer, so a foreground wait does not
   block until the phase finishes: it dies at the cap and reports exit `2` on a phase that is
   still running healthily. You then re-run it, burning a turn and a fresh context read every
   10 minutes. Backgrounding removes the cap — one wait, one wake-up, when the phase is
   actually done. It is also the only way a `--timeout-ms` above 600 000 is reachable at all.

   **The rule the old "always foreground" advice was protecting still holds**, and it is the
   part that matters: *never do your own work while a phase agent is writing.* That is drovr's
   single-writer rule, not a property of foreground-ness. Backgrounding is only dangerous if
   you keep working — so background the wait and go idle.

   This POLLS the filesystem for the marker the agent drops via `drovr phase done` (step 2's
   final action). Completion is that marker, never herdr's `idle` status — `idle` also fires
   while the agent is parked awaiting a reviewer or explorer of its own. **Note the default
   `--timeout-ms` is 30 000 (30 s), which is far too short for a real phase; always pass an
   explicit value.** Pass a long one — 86 400 000 (24 h) above: exit `2` only ever means
   "re-arm", and every re-arm is a turn spent learning nothing. A blocked agent ends the wait
   with exit `4` long before any timeout; what a long timeout gives up is noticing an agent that
   sits idle without finishing, so look at `drovr status <run>` if a phase is taking far longer
   than its work should.

   Handle the exit code the wake-up hands you:

   | Exit | Meaning | What to do |
   |---|---|---|
   | `0` | done — the handoff exists | Go to step 4. |
   | `4` | **blocked** — the agent hit a safety/permission prompt; the diagnostic names the class | Answer the prompt (`herdr agent send-keys <pane> …`), then **re-arm**. Do not treat this as failure. |
   | `2` | timed out; the phase may still be running healthily | **Re-arm**, or investigate if it has now timed out twice. |
   | `5` | **superseded** — a newer `phase start` re-entered the phase while this wait ran, so it was watching a pass that no longer exists | Nothing is wrong with the phase. **Re-arm** to follow the live pass. Never triage this as a stuck agent. |
   | `1` | I/O error | STOP — see *Stop conditions*. |

   ⚠️ **Do not pipe this command.** A shell pipeline's exit status is its **last** command's,
   so `drovr phase wait … | tail -5` reports `tail`'s 0 and every row above reads as `0` —
   done. Trimming output with `| tail`/`| head`/`| grep` is a natural habit and it voids this
   table silently. Capture the status instead:
   ```
   drovr phase wait <run> <phase> --timeout-ms 86400000; rc=$?; echo "EXIT=$rc"; exit $rc
   ```
   The same trap applies to every drovr command with an exit-code contract — `review wait`
   and `code-review run` most of all, where a swallowed status has already produced both a
   false approval and a false clean review.

   **Re-arm** = run the exact same backgrounded `drovr phase wait` again and end the turn again.
   The wait is stateless and resumable: it polls an on-disk marker, so nothing is lost by
   re-issuing it and a phase that finished during the gap is detected immediately.

   **`phase wait` only sees the phase you named.** It is the right tool while you are driving one
   phase and have nothing else in flight. When several agents are running — a panel, or two phases
   across two runs — background `drovr watch [<run>]` instead (or as well): it exits `4` the moment
   ANY of them stops on a prompt only a human can answer, and `0` when every agent has exited.
   Answer the prompt, then re-arm exactly as above. A `drovr ask` never ends it — a question is
   the human's to answer on the run's page, not yours — it only keeps the watch from exiting `0`.

4. **Collect + hand forward.**
   ```
   drovr collect <run> <phase>
   ```
   Prints the handoff (the file the agent authored). It becomes the next phase's
   `--context-file` in step 1 — drovr puts it in the brief it composes.

## Quick reference

| Step | Command | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **start (briefed)** | `drovr phase start <run> <phase> --context-file <prev handoff>` | composes the brief AND injects it; prints `briefed phase …`. Exit 2 = pane up but unbriefed |
| inspect | `drovr phase brief <run> <phase> [--context …]` | prints exactly what the agent is told, spawning nothing |
| re-brief | `drovr phase brief … \| drovr phase send <run> <phase> -` | for a phase already running; `phase send "<text>"` is for free-form nudges only |
| wait | `drovr phase wait <run> <phase> --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded, then end the turn**; polls for the `done` marker (not herdr idle). `0`=done → step 4 · `4`=blocked on a prompt → answer it, re-arm · `2`=timeout → re-arm · `5`=superseded by a newer pass → re-arm, not a stuck agent · `1`=io-error → stop. Default timeout is only 30 s — always override. Foreground Bash caps at 600 000 ms, so a foreground wait times out on healthy long phases |
| watch | `drovr watch [<run>] --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded**; exits when ANY agent (of the run, or of every run drovr can read) stops on a prompt drovr will not answer. `4`=needs a human, the report names the phase and quotes the prompt · `0`=nothing left to watch (every agent gone, every run's phases finished, AND no unanswered `drovr ask`) — an unanswered ask never ends the watch and is never reported, it only holds it open · `2`=timeout → re-arm · `1`=error, including any run whose state could not be read. Routine permission dialogs do not wake it — a running `phase wait` answers those. Safe to background BEFORE `phase start`: a run with phases outstanding keeps it watching |
| ask | `drovr ask <run> --question <text\|@file> [--context <text> \| --context-file <path> \| --context-html <path>] [--option <value>=<label>]... [--recommend <value>]` | run by the AGENT, never the driver: posts one question for the human and **returns immediately** — it never blocks and never waits. Prints three lines — the ask id, the reviewer's page URL (starting the review server if it is not already up; only a server that could not be started gets a note instead, and the question is on disk either way), and the `ask wait` command to background. `0`=posted · `5`=run cancelled (terminal — stop work, do not re-ask) · `1`=error. `--context`/`--context-file`/`--context-html` are mutually exclusive. `--context-html` takes a FILE of HTML — headings, tables, a `<style>` block — shown in a sandboxed frame beside the question, for a decision a paragraph of plain text renders badly. It is REFUSED, exit `1`, if the file does not parse, and the accepted subset is narrower than a browser's: every element closed, attributes quoted, `<` for a bare `<`, no script. `drovr ask preview <path>` runs the same check and writes the rendered document to a temp file you can open — use it before posting, not after. `@<path>` on `--question` reads the text from a file (`@@` escapes a leading `@`). The record is append-only in `<run_dir>/interview.jsonl`, so it survives the agent that posted it |
| ask wait | `drovr ask wait <run> --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded, then end the turn**; a file poller, so it works while the panel is down. `0`=every question it was armed on is answered — those asks, each with its latest answer, as JSON on stdout (**not** the whole log; earlier answered asks are not in it) · `2`=timeout → re-arm, **nothing is lost** (the question is still on disk and still on screen) · `5`=run cancelled · `1`=error, including a run dir that is not there. Nothing pending at start also exits `0`, and that case prints the whole folded interview rather than a bare `[]` |
| done | `drovr phase done <run> <phase>` | run by the AGENT as its final action; **refuses until `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` exists**; drops the marker `wait` polls |
| scaffold | `drovr handoff-scaffold <run> <phase>` | writes the empty 7 sections for the AGENT to fill; refuses to overwrite an authored one. Structure only — drovr does not guess which commits are yours. `phase done` refuses while any section is still `TODO` |
| collect | `drovr collect <run> <phase>` | reads `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` |

## The HANDOFF doc shape

The finishing agent authors a fixed 7-section document (objective · state · decisions+rationale ·
interfaces/contracts · open questions · next step · artifact pointers). See
`HANDOFF-template.md` in this directory for the contract and what each section is for.
**Artifact pointers are paths, not pasted content** — the next agent re-reads source on
demand (that is what keeps each phase's context small). Artifact pointers **must include git
references** — the branch and the commit range/SHAs carrying this phase's work — so the next
agent re-derives load-bearing decisions from `git log`/`git diff`, using history as a durable
cross-check against lossy compression rather than trusting the summary alone.

## Self-review before you author the handoff

If the phase produced an artifact (code, a spec, a plan), the phase agent should have
**reviewed its own work with read-only reviewers** and addressed their
Critical/Important findings *before* authoring the handoff and handing forward. Read-only
reviewers preserve the single-writer rule — they find, the phase agent fixes. Compressing an
unreviewed artifact just carries its defects into the next phase's briefing. (The
`drovr:pipeline` phase-prompts encode this per phase.)

## Stop conditions — a bad handoff cascades

If any of these happen, **STOP and surface diagnostics** rather than seeding the next phase
with a broken briefing:

- `drovr phase wait` exits `1` (failed) or keeps exiting `2` (never completes).
- `drovr phase done` keeps failing because the agent never authored the handoff, or
  `drovr collect` returns empty / missing the fixed sections.

Diagnose with `herdr agent read <pane>` (raw transcript), or `drovr attach <run>` to inspect
the pane live.
Seeding a fresh agent from a garbage handoff wastes the whole downstream chain — a broken
briefing is worse than a stopped run.

**Not a stop condition: `phase done` refusing with `$DROVR_PASS is not set`.** The marker must
carry the pass token the agent was launched under, so `drovr phase done` only works from inside
the phase's own pane. Run by hand from a plain shell it refuses — and prints the exact command
that would work, token included. The general form, for when you are composing it yourself:

```
DROVR_PASS=$(jq -r '.phases[]|select(.name=="<phase>").pass' <run_dir>/state.json) \
  drovr phase done <run> <phase>
```

`<run_dir>` is `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>`; a reviewer phase lives under
`.review_phases[]` instead. This is the escape hatch for a phase whose agent is gone but whose
work is finished — it bypasses the pane, not the contract: `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` must still
exist, with no `TODO` sections left.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Writing the brief yourself | drovr composes it. You supply `--context`; `phase brief` shows the result. A hand-written frame drifts from the contract and nothing detects it. |
| Ignoring exit 2 from `phase start` | The pane is up and UNBRIEFED. Re-deliver with `phase brief \| phase send -`; a `phase wait` on it never returns. |
| Expecting a separate compress step | There isn't one. The finishing agent authors the handoff itself, as its final action, before `phase done`. |
| `phase done` failing "handoff missing" | The agent must author `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` *before* running `phase done`; the marker won't drop without it. |
| `phase done` naming sections "still at the scaffold's TODO" | A scaffolded handoff was never filled in. Write those sections from your own context — nothing else will — then re-run. |
| Foregrounding `drovr phase wait` | Background it and end the turn. Foreground Bash is capped at 600 000 ms, so a long healthy phase reports a false exit `2`. |
| Backgrounding the wait and then working | Background the wait *and go idle*. The single-writer rule is what forbids working here, not foreground-ness. |
| Pasting file contents into the handoff | Use artifact pointers (paths + git refs); the successor re-reads. |
| Hardcoding `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` elsewhere | Read it via `drovr collect`; the finishing agent writes it directly (no CLI command authors it). |

# HANDOFF: package the Orca GUI without the bwrap FHS sandbox

## 1. Objective

Replace `appimageTools.wrapType2` (a bubblewrap FHS sandbox) for the Orca GUI in
`orca.nix` with an unsandboxed package: the AppImage's extracted tree patched with
`autoPatchelfHook` and wrapped with `makeWrapper`, the way nixpkgs packages most
closed-source Electron apps (slack, discord, vscode). Done = the GUI runs on shiori
(Arch + Hyprland, no X server, non-NixOS) unsandboxed, is merged to master, and is
switched in with `hms`.

Why: the sandbox is the root of a run of bugs.
- Everything Orca spawns (its terminals, and the agents in them, this one included)
  lives inside it. `/etc/hostname` is missing, `date` prints UTC (`/etc/localtime`
  -> host file -> `/usr/share/zoneinfo`, which the sandbox's `/usr` replaces), and
  `/usr` is not Arch's.
- Fonts dangled the same way (every family fell to Montserrat Thin). The `fontsConf`
  workaround and `tests/sandbox-fonts.sh` exist only because of that.
- bwrap sits between every caller and the process and forwards no signals, and its
  `--die-with-parent` SIGKILLs the payload when its parent goes.

The original comment in `orca.nix` chose the sandbox because it "works on non-NixOS
hosts". That reason does not hold: a patchelf'd binary references store paths and
runs on Arch fine.

## 2. State

- master's `orca.nix`:
  - The GUI is `wrapType2` + nixGL. The bin is `orca-ide`, a wrapper that always adds
    `--ozone-platform=wayland`.
  - It has `extraBwrapArgs` for `FONTCONFIG_FILE=fontsConf`.
  - It has master's Mac-keybinding table and activation, which use `appimageContents`
    (extracted AppImage) for `app.asar`. Leave that work alone.
- **A parallel change is landing on master from another Orca session (the CLI work),
  touching the same file:**
  - `orca-ide` and `orca` become Orca's CLI, run on nixpkgs nodejs as
    `node ${appimageContents}/resources/app.asar.unpacked/out/cli/index.js`. No sandbox.
  - The GUI is renamed to `orca-ide-app`. The desktop Exec uses it, and so does
    `meta.mainProgram`.
  - The CLI env sets `ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE` to the GUI's `orca-ide-app`, so
    `orca-ide open` launches it.
  - Six Orca skills go into `~/.claude/skills`.

  Do not implement any of that here. Before merging, **rebase or merge onto
  origin/master and keep the GUI bin named `orca-ide-app`** (if the CLI change has
  landed by then).
- Nothing has been built for this task yet.

## 3. Decisions + rationale (already made, with the user)

- **Unsandbox the GUI with autoPatchelf; do not keep bwrap.**
- **Keep nixGL** (`config.lib.nixGL.wrap`). Without it, GBM/DRI look in the
  NixOS-only `/run/opengl-driver` and fall back to software rendering.
- **Keep the Wayland flag, conditional:** add `--ozone-platform=wayland` only when
  `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` is unset.
  - Hyprland has no X server, and Orca's startup gate picks X11 without it: a bare
    launch exits 1 with "needs a usable display server".
  - Node rejects the flag ("bad option", exit 9), and the CLI's `serve` probes
    `ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE` in node mode with a script as argv.
  - It also must not be injected into CLI dispatch. Master's always-on flag breaks
    `orca-ide open`: "Unknown flag --ozone-platform for command: open".
- **Plain exec wrapper only.** No shell that backgrounds the process, no signal
  forwarding. Unsandboxed, signals and exit codes reach Electron directly. That is
  the point of this change.
- Expect `fontsConf` / FONTCONFIG_FILE and `tests/sandbox-fonts.sh` to become
  unnecessary. With the host's `/usr` visible, fontconfig should see the host config.
  Verify before deleting either: Orca's default terminal font must still resolve to
  exactly "DejaVu Sans Mono" (`dejavu_fonts`).
- Electron's runtime needs: libsecret (safeStorage).

## 4. Interfaces / contracts

- The extracted AppImage (`pkgs.appimageTools.extract { inherit pname version src; }`)
  has:
  - `orca-ide`: the Electron binary.
  - `chrome-sandbox`, `chrome_crashpad_handler`, and the `.so`s next to them.
  - `resources/`, with more native ELF helpers that each need their libraries
    resolved: `orcad-template`, `relay`, `agent-browser-linux-x64`,
    `computer-use-linux`, `ripgrep`, `node-runtime`, `bin/orca-wayland-clipboard`,
    plus `app.asar.unpacked` native modules. Run `find -type f -exec file` to list
    them all.
- **chrome-sandbox:** Nix cannot make it setuid. Upstream's postinst only does that
  for hosts without unprivileged user namespaces; Arch has them. Confirm Chromium
  uses the namespace sandbox, and, if needed, decide between `--no-sandbox` and
  removing `chrome-sandbox` so it does not try the SUID path. Escalate to the user
  rather than silently disabling the Chromium sandbox.
- Desktop file: `orca-ide.desktop` with `Exec=AppRun %U` upstream. Rewrite Exec to
  the GUI bin. The scheme handler `x-scheme-handler/orca` must keep working. Install
  the hicolor icons 16..512 as now.
- Upstream's own `.deb` layout, for reference: `/usr/bin/orca-ide` -> CLI shim; GUI
  at `/opt/Orca/orca-ide`, not on PATH; desktop file `Exec=/opt/Orca/orca-ide %U`.

## 5. Open questions

- Does `autoPatchelfHook` resolve every helper in `resources/`? Some may dlopen libs
  (libGL/EGL, libsecret, libnotify) that need `runtimeDependencies` or
  `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.
- Does the bundled `node-runtime` / `orcad-template` need anything beyond patching?
  `orca-ide serve` uses orcad.
- Is `fontsConf` removable? Measure with fc-match from inside the running app's
  terminal.
- **CAUTION, you are running inside Orca.** Restarting or replacing the running Orca
  kills your own session. Test the new build as a second instance with its own
  profile, e.g. `--user-data-dir=$(mktemp -d)`, never by restarting the live app.
  Per the user's memory notes, eval-green plus a launched process is not "working":
  force a real render (open a window, a terminal tab) and check `coredumpctl` for
  crashes.

## 6. Next step

1. Create a branch in this worktree. Per memory, edits go in a worktree, never main
   on master.
2. Write a test first in `tests/`, committed to the repo per memory. It should fail
   now and pass after. Suggested claims:
   - the GUI bin is not a bwrap launcher;
   - `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 <gui> -p 1` prints 1;
   - `ldd` (or `patchelf --print-needed` plus resolution) of every ELF under the
     package has no "not found";
   - a launched second instance, with its own `--user-data-dir`, reports
     `TZ`/`date` and `/etc/hostname` as the host does, from a process it spawns.
3. Implement.
4. Review with drovr:code-review, to two consecutive clean rounds on an unchanged
   HEAD. No round cap; the user was explicit about that.
   - If the drovr panel can't run (it needs herdr; inside Orca it exits 1 on
     HERDR_SOCKET_PATH), use two read-only Explore reviewer agents per round
     instead: correctness+error-handling, and security+quality.
5. Merge to master, re-checking master first. Per memory, merge without asking.
6. Run `hms` (bare, never piped). Never `hms --local` unasked.

## 7. Artifact pointers

- Repo: `~/devel/dotfiles`. The file is `orca.nix`; it is imported from `home.nix`.
- master at the time of writing: `git log origin/master -- orca.nix`. Keybinding work
  is in `nix/orca-mac-keybindings*.js` and `tests/orca-mac-keybindings.sh`.
- Research branch `orca-cli-skills` at worktree
  `~/devel/dotfiles/.drovr/wt/orca-cli-skills`. It is being superseded, but its
  commit messages record what the sandbox broke, round by round:
  `git log origin/master..orca-cli-skills`. 9e53e6cc..d892f61a carry the findings;
  `tests/orca-cli-skills.sh` there has node-mode and signal probes worth reusing as
  checks that an unsandboxed build gets right for free.
- Upstream .deb (v1.4.238): https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/download/v1.4.238/orca-ide_1.4.238_amd64.deb
  Its `postinst` shows the CLI symlink and `chmod 4755 chrome-sandbox`.
- Release feed (version + sha512 source of truth):
  https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/latest-linux.yml

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for the claims orca.nix makes about the Orca CLI and its agent skills:
# that `orca-ide` and `orca` are the CLI and run from any shell, not only an
# Orca terminal; that the GUI is `orca-ide-app` and the CLI can launch it; and
# that the skills in ~/.claude/skills are the bytes this Orca build expects.
#
# Why this needs a test. Orca's own installer only reaches an Orca terminal: it
# puts a shim dir on PATH there (ORCA_CLI_BIN_DIR) and symlinks
# ~/.local/bin/orca-ide at a raw /nix/store path, a script that runs Electron
# against the host's libraries. The skills are stubs that tell the agent to
# run `orca-ide skills get <name>` outside an Orca terminal, so a skill without
# a working CLI under that name is a dead end. And the skills are pinned to a
# commit separately from the AppImage version; bumping one without the other
# silently installs guides for a different CLI. Orca ships the expected hashes
# in resources/skills/current-manifest.json, so that is what the files are
# held to.
#
# Usage:
#   tests/orca-cli-skills.sh    eval + build this host's config and test it

set -u
set -o pipefail

fails=0; n=0
pass() { n=$((n+1)); echo "ok   $1"; }
fail() { n=$((n+1)); echo "FAIL $1: $2"; fails=$((fails+1)); }
T=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$T"' EXIT

FLAKE=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)
# /etc/hostname is what CI writes to say which host it is; Orca's sandbox does
# not bind it in, so fall back to uname -n there.
HM="$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$(cat /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null || uname -n).config"
SKILLS="orca-cli orchestration computer-use orca-per-workspace-env orca-linear linear-tickets"

pkg_attr() { # pkg_attr <pname> <attr>
  nix eval --raw "$HM.home.packages" \
    --apply "ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: (p.pname or \"\") == \"$1\") ps)).$2"
}
drv=$(pkg_attr orca-cli drvPath) || { echo "no orca-cli in home.packages here" >&2; exit 1; }
want_version=$(pkg_attr orca-cli version) && [ -n "$want_version" ] \
  || { echo "orca-cli has no version" >&2; exit 1; }
CLI=$(nix-store --realise "$drv" | tail -1) || { echo "could not build orca-cli" >&2; exit 1; }
gui_drv=$(pkg_attr orca drvPath) || { echo "no orca in home.packages here" >&2; exit 1; }
GUI=$(nix-store --realise "$gui_drv" | tail -1) || { echo "could not build orca" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $CLI and $GUI"

# The skills' own rule: outside an Orca terminal, on Linux, the CLI is
# `orca-ide`; elsewhere it is `orca`. Both names must be the CLI, and the GUI
# must not also claim `orca-ide` -- in the profile it would shadow one of them.
for b in orca orca-ide; do
  if [ -x "$CLI/bin/$b" ]; then pass "orca-cli provides bin/$b"
  else fail "bin/$b" "missing from $CLI"; fi
done
if [ -x "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" ] && [ ! -e "$GUI/bin/orca-ide" ]; then
  pass "the GUI is orca-ide-app and leaves orca-ide to the CLI"
else fail "GUI bin names" "$(ls "$GUI/bin" | paste -sd' ')"; fi

# No sandbox between the caller and the CLI: a plain exec of node, so
# signals and exit codes are the CLI's own.
if grep -q 'exec .*/bin/node ' "$CLI/bin/orca-ide" && ! grep -q bwrap "$CLI/bin/orca-ide"; then
  pass "the CLI is a plain exec of node"
else fail "CLI launcher" "$CLI/bin/orca-ide is not a plain node exec"; fi

# `orca-ide open` spawns ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE, or else process.execPath --
# which under plain node is node itself. Exactly the profile's GUI: the
# unwrapped one has an orca-ide-app too, minus nixGL.
app=$(sed -nE 's|.*ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE:-([^}]*)\}.*|\1|p' "$CLI/bin/orca-ide")
if [ "$app" = "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" ]; then
  pass "orca open launches the profile's nixGL-wrapped GUI"
else fail "ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE" "'${app:-unset}', want $GUI/bin/orca-ide-app"; fi

# The GUI's --ozone-platform=wayland must stay out of node mode: the CLI's
# `serve` probes ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE with ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 and a
# script as argv, and Node rejects the flag ("bad option", exit 9).
out=$(ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 timeout 60 "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" -p '"node-ok"' 2>"$T/node-err")
if [ "$out" = node-ok ]; then
  pass "orca-ide-app runs in node mode (serve's runtime probe)"
else fail "orca-ide-app node mode" "${out:-$(tail -1 "$T/node-err")}"; fi

# `orca-ide open` spawns the GUI detached, then exits. Each GUI wrapper layer
# execs the next, so the GUI's bwrap is the CLI's own child; with
# --die-with-parent it would be SIGKILLed the moment `open` returns.
bash -c 'ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$1" -e "
  setTimeout(() => require(\"fs\").writeFileSync(process.argv[1], \"alive\"), 3000);
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 4000);" "$2" >/dev/null 2>&1 &' _ "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" "$T/alive"
for _ in $(seq 75); do [ -s "$T/alive" ] && break; sleep 0.2; done
if [ -s "$T/alive" ]; then pass "the GUI outlives the parent that spawned it (orca-ide open)"
else fail "GUI lifetime" "payload died with its spawning parent"; fi

# The manifest travels with the extracted AppImage, which the CLI's script
# references, so it is in the CLI's closure.
contents=$(nix-store -qR "$CLI" | while read -r p; do
  [ -f "$p/resources/skills/current-manifest.json" ] && echo "$p"; done | head -1)
[ -n "$contents" ] || { echo "no extracted AppImage in the closure of $CLI" >&2; exit 1; }
manifest="$contents/resources/skills/current-manifest.json"

# Outside an Orca terminal: none of its env, none of its shim dir on PATH.
# ${!ORCA_@}, not compgen: CI's bash is built without programmable completion.
clean_path=$(printf '%s' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | grep -v 'linux-orca-cli-shim' | paste -sd:)
outside() {
  local u=() v
  for v in ${!ORCA_@}; do u+=(-u "$v"); done
  env "${u[@]}" PATH="$clean_path" "$@"
}

got=$(outside "$CLI/bin/orca" --version 2>&1)
if printf '%s' "$got" | grep -qwF "$want_version"; then pass "orca --version reports $want_version outside Orca"
else fail "orca --version" "got '$got', want $want_version"; fi

# What every skill stub runs, under both names the stubs choose between.
for b in orca-ide orca; do
  got=$(outside "$CLI/bin/$b" skills get orca-cli 2>&1)
  if printf '%s' "$got" | grep -q '^# Orca CLI'; then pass "$b skills get orca-cli prints the guide outside Orca"
  else fail "$b skills get" "$(printf '%s' "$got" | head -3)"; fi
done

# A CLI failure is the CLI's exit status, not swallowed by a wrapper.
outside "$CLI/bin/orca-ide" no-such-command >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?
if [ "$rc" -eq 1 ]; then pass "an unknown command exits 1"
else fail "exit status" "unknown command exited $rc"; fi

# The rev is pinned by hand next to the version; the app knows its own.
rev=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply 'f: f.".claude/skills/orca-cli".source' | sed -nE 's|.*-orca-skills-([0-9a-f]{40})/.*|\1|p')
if [ -n "$rev" ] && grep -aqF "sourceCommit:\`$rev\`" "$contents/resources/app.asar"; then
  pass "skills rev ${rev:0:8} is this build's sourceCommit"
else fail "skills rev" "'${rev:-unparsed}' is not the sourceCommit in app.asar"; fi

for s in $SKILLS; do
  src=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply "f: toString f.\".claude/skills/$s\".source" 2>/dev/null) \
    || { fail "$s" "no home.file .claude/skills/$s"; continue; }
  # The source is a subpath of a fetch; realise the fetch's derivation itself.
  srcdrv=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply \
    "f: builtins.head (builtins.attrNames (builtins.getContext f.\".claude/skills/$s\".source))" 2>/dev/null)
  nix-store --realise "$srcdrv" >/dev/null
  # Every file the manifest lists for the skill, as "<sha256>  <path>" lines.
  want=$(jq -r --arg n "$s" '.skills[] | select(.name == $n) | .files[] | "\(.exactSha256)  \(.path)"' "$manifest")
  [ -n "$want" ] || { fail "$s" "no entry in the manifest"; continue; }
  if out=$(cd "$src" 2>/dev/null && printf '%s\n' "$want" | sha256sum --quiet -c - 2>&1); then
    pass "$s matches this build's manifest ($(printf '%s\n' "$want" | wc -l) files)"
  else fail "$s" "${out:-$src is missing}"; fi
done

printf '\n%d/%d passed\n' "$((n-fails))" "$n"
[ "$fails" -eq 0 ]

**What changed:**
1. **The test can't open a stray Orca window.** The two checks that launch the GUI binary now run with no display set. If node mode ever broke, the launch would stop at Orca's display check instead of opening a window.
